turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, both of you. I'm Dr Shah. Lovely to see you — what's been going on?
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm his daughter, I live in with him. It's the legs, doctor. They've ballooned again.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): The legs. How are you feeling in yourself?
[SEG0004] person_3 (PATIENT): Swollen.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Both sides, or just one?
[SEG0006] person_3 (PATIENT): Both.
[SEG0007] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry, he won't give you a paragraph. Last couple of weeks, and by evening his shoes won't go on. We nearly missed the bus, the 47 was late again.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): The shoes are useful to know. Any breathlessness with the swelling?
[SEG0009] person_3 (PATIENT): Stairs.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): On the stairs. And sitting quietly — breathless then, or no?
[SEG0011] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0012] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He stops halfway up now. He never used to.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain while that's happening?
[SEG0014] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): What about a cough, or a wheeze?
[SEG0016] person_3 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0017] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He still sleeps flat. No extra pillows. I'd have noticed, I'm in the next room.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's good to hear. How's your energy, and your appetite?
[SEG0019] person_3 (PATIENT): Tired.
[SEG0020] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He eats everything I cook. It's the tiredness. And he nods off in the armchair after lunch, every day lately.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): You sort the pill box, don't you? Talk me through it.
[SEG0022] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sunday nights. The water tablet first — box says furosemide. Forty milligrams, one in the morning.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): And he actually takes that one?
[SEG0024] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I put it out and he swallows it. I haven't seen him miss it.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): What else sits in the morning compartment?
[SEG0026] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Bisoprolol, two and a half milligrams. His heart tablet. Then the little white one.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any name on the little white one?
[SEG0028] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Nothing I can read, it's tiny and round. I think it's the blood pressure tablet, maybe five milligrams? I binned the box, which was stupid of me.
[SEG0029] person_3 (PATIENT): White.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): So no name we can trust. Is bisoprolol separate from the heart tablet, or have you counted one tablet twice?
[SEG0031] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Oh. Um. I've double-counted it. The heart tablet is the bisoprolol. There's only one.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll log it once, then. Two and a half, mornings. Did another doctor stop anything?
[SEG0033] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Atorvastatin, the cholesterol one. Hospital doctor stopped it in March. His legs were aching.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): And he's stayed off it?
[SEG0035] person_3 (PATIENT): Yes.
[SEG0036] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes. They wrote naproxen for his knee as well, but we never collected it. He never took one.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Naproxen never started, so I'll ignore that. Any shop-bought pain relief?
[SEG0038] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Paracetamol, when the knee grumbles. Not daily.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Roughly how much, and how often?
[SEG0040] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Two tablets, maybe two or three times a week. Five hundred milligrams each, I think. Boots own.
[SEG0041] person_3 (PATIENT): Knee.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does the knee still play up?
[SEG0043] person_3 (PATIENT): Sometimes.
[SEG0044] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Old arthritis, years of it. Not why we're here. His brother had a knee done — oh, ignore that, not relevant.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Consider it ignored. The heart failure and the blood pressure — those are still the diagnoses you've been living with?
[SEG0046] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Yes. Heart failure a few years back, and high blood pressure. Both still going on.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look at those ankles and listen in.
[SEG0048] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Worse on the left, I reckon. Or — actually, maybe not. Hard to tell in the morning.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Both ankles are puffy and they pit with pressure. Chest is clear, no crackles. Heart sounds are normal, no murmur. Pulse is seventy-two, regular.
[SEG0050] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the blood pressure?
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): One hundred and thirty-eight over eighty-two. Oxygen saturation is ninety-six percent.
[SEG0052] person_3 (PATIENT): Alright.

[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): I think the puffy ankles and getting breathless on the stairs mean the heart failure is a little less settled. I'd like to change the water tablet. Forty milligrams once a day isn't holding the swelling, so we'll give forty milligrams in the morning and another forty at lunchtime.
[SEG0054] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So two of them?

[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Two doses, yes — not both at once. Leave the bisoprolol as it is. And I won't guess at the little white one. Bring the tablet itself, or a clear photo, before we touch it.
[SEG0056] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll photograph it tonight.

[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the breathing gets worse, or he can't lie flat, or the swelling shoots up, come straight back, don't wait. Otherwise I'll see you in two weeks to see if the extra dose has done the job.
[SEG0058] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Two weeks is fine.
[SEG0059] person_3 (PATIENT): Ta.

omissions.text: The unidentified 'little white' morning tablet should not be recorded as a current medication with dose 5 mg; the daughter explicitly said she only guessed it might be the blood pressure tablet and the doctor said there was no name they could trust and not to guess at it.

Heart sounds were normal on examination.
The doctor advised not to take both extra furosemide doses at once.
